content: Polyuria is defined as a urine output exceeding 2 liters per 24 hours or 30 milliliters per kilogram per 24 hours. The pathophysiological causes of polyuria can be categorized into three main groups: increased thirst (which may be idiopathic, psychogenic polydipsia, hypothalamic disease, or medication-induced), central diabetes insipidus (resulting from decreased secretion of arginine vasopressin, or AVP), and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (caused by renal resistance to AVP). Life-threatening causes of polyuria are not identified, as polyuria itself does not directly lead to conditions that may result in death or permanent disability within 24 hours if untreated. The most common causes of polyuria include pregnancy, psychogenic polydipsia, central diabetes insipidus (CDI), nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI), diabetes mellitus (DM), chronic kidney disease (CKD), urinary tract infection (UTI), interstitial cystitis, nephrolithiasis, primary hyperparathyroidism, familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, sickle cell disease (SCD), stroke or other neurological diseases, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), stress incontinence, and certain medications such as lithium and diuretics. Other contributing factors include an overactive bladder, alcohol consumption, and caffeine intake. The diagnostic approach to polyuria involves an algorithmic evaluation, as outlined in the American Journal of Kidney Diseases, which helps to identify the underlying cause of the condition. The treatment of polyuria is tailored to address its underlying cause. For example, psychogenic polydipsia, diabetes insipidus (both central and nephrogenic), and diabetes mellitus (types 1 and 2) each require specific management strategies. Dietary modifications are recommended to avoid bladder irritants such as caffeine, alcohol, carbonated drinks, tomato-based products, chocolate, artificial sweeteners, and spicy foods. Patients should monitor their fluid and food intake, ensuring adequate hydration to prevent constipation and overly concentrated urine, while avoiding excessive fluid intake before bedtime. Kegel exercises are advised to strengthen the muscles surrounding the bladder and urethra, which may help improve bladder control.
